s01.slug: MONDAY · 7:50 AM · ANACAPA COMMONS — MYSTERY GUY
body: It is the first Monday in two weeks without rain on it, and the Commons has put the patio tables back out the way a town puts out flags, each one wiped down by somebody who didn’t want to be the one who hadn’t, the undersides still beaded. The sprinklers on the lawn have come back on, Marisol’s way of announcing that it believes the weather. Jack has the table nearest the glass doors, in the sun, with the Carhartt over the back of the chair and a plate of eggs he has had four peaceful bites of.
The RAZR goes off against the tabletop at 7:44, and goes off again, and then keeps going in a run, as it does for exactly one person at this hour.

body: He doesn’t answer the last one. He holds the phone open until the screen goes dark by itself, and his other hand goes back over the chair to the Carhartt and stays on the collar.

Kevin and Margot are across from him, Kevin with his oatmeal and a banana he is cutting into thirds with the edge of a spoon, Margot with her hot water and a legal pad she hasn’t opened. Neither has asked why he is holding the RAZR in his hand like something that might bite. It’s Monday. People are allowed to look at a phone.

Theo comes across the patio at ten of eight with the iPhone held out in front of him like a hymnal. The gold pin is on the lapel of the blazer; Hollis, retired with honors, is back in his teacup on the nightstand in 412. A brother since Saturday, Theo is insufferable before nine in a way he had to be taught, and he has evidently been up since six waiting for somebody to ask him why, and no one has. He sets the phone down by the butter, turns it a quarter turn toward Jack with one finger, and sits.

“Good morning, Costigan. Please remain seated.” He reads the headline in the voice that comes right before the weather. “‘Sweetwater’s Skye Callender marches with pro-lifers — and who’s her mystery guy?’” He looks up. “They don’t know. It’s the one honest sentence on the internet.”
He scrolls it for the table a photograph at a time.

body: Jack has been photographed at his Confirmation and for the Mooney yearbook, and never from behind, by strangers, with a caption. Under the item the comments begin, and Theo, unasked, reads three of them in three voices. “‘Mystery Guy looks like he’s about to apologize to a nun,’” in a woman’s alto. “‘That’s not a Catholic school boy, that’s a Teamster,’” in a baritone, from a user called UnionMaid4Life. And in a breathless soprano, from a user who has not read the item: “‘is he single.’”

The phone goes around. Kevin reads it with both thumbs and goes the color of his oatmeal. “There’s a thread,” he says. “About the jacket. Somebody’s linked the catalog.” He scrolls. “In fairness, it’s the right model.” He hands the phone on quickly. “My GPA was on the internet once. In high school. It was a typo — somebody transposed a nine — and it took a semester to come down, and in that semester a girl in my AP Chem lab stopped lending me her good pen. I want you to know I understand.”

Margot takes it last and reads it through to the end with her hot water going cold at her elbow, wearing the face she keeps for a field report. “The internet has identified you by your outerwear,” she says, and slides the phone back to Theo. “In my discipline that’s called material culture. You are a garment, Costigan. Congratulations.” She regards him. “Do you own another coat? As a matter of method.”
“It’s January.”
“He has one coat,” Theo says. “It isn’t a wardrobe, it’s a vow.”
Kevin wants a statement drafted. “Short. Dignified. Nothing about the jacket.”
“No statements,” says Theo. “The first rule of Mystery Guy is that he doesn’t know he’s Mystery Guy.”

Doug Pruitt arrives with a tray of hash browns and his own phone already out, and stops at the end of the table as if somebody had hung a velvet rope there. “Dude,” he says, in all five vowels. “You’re *Mystery Guy*.”
“I’m aware.”

“A girl in the omelet line showed me. I said, *dude, he’s got that jacket*, and she said, ‘That’s the whole point,’ and I still didn’t get it till I sat down.” He sits. “That’s so weird. You’re like a ghost that has a coat.”

“Kenzie’s very proud of the album,” Kevin says. He has put his spoon down for it. “She doesn’t know it’s public. I’m going to tell her. Gently. Today.” He takes a folded index card out of his shirt pocket and consults it. “I have notes.”
At 7:58 the RAZR lights on the table, and this one he picks up.

body: Doug asks if it’s Gina. “It’s Skye,” Jack says. “I’m required at a lunch.”
“Is that, like, an honor, dude?”
“It’s an interview with bread.”

By the cereal bar a table of Louisiana kids who have been up since six for no reason but joy puts one of its members on a chair, and he calls it — *Who dat?* — and the Commons answers, even the omelet line, two weeks out from Miami. Jack keeps his eyes on the eggs. He doesn’t look toward the window tables.
Theo wipes the iPhone’s screen on his lapel and lays it face down. “As your roommate, your friend and a man with a pin,” he says, “what do we do about Mystery Guy?”

response: “Brass,” Theo says at once, and the hand with the pin goes up and cuts the air, already seeing it. “A serif. MYSTERY GUY, EST. 2010. I’ll have it by Friday.”
“Brass is a choice,” says Margot.

Doug wants to know whether it goes on the door of 412 or on the door of the Commons, and Theo says that is the kind of question that wins grants. Kevin, who has been waiting for someone to ask him to be reasonable, asks whether a plaque is the best response to a thread. “It is the only response,” says Theo, “that comes with a ceremony.”
The table goes quiet. Doug has a hash brown halfway to his mouth. “Who’s Danny?”
Theo, who sat across a table from Danny on Christmas Eve with a bag of vending-machine pretzels between them, doesn’t look at Jack. “His brother,” he says, short. “It’s a very good jacket.”
Kevin slides his tray across the table until it touches Jack’s, and eats his oatmeal. Doug lowers the hash brown.

Jack closes the RAZR and picks up his fork. Doug, who has never been refused a screen in his life, takes Theo’s iPhone off the table and reads the comments aloud instead, with feeling — a woman’s indignation, a man’s theory about the tan of the Carhartt — until Kevin lifts the phone out of his hand. “That’s enough of the public.”
“The public was just getting interesting,” says Margot, and goes back to her hot water, aggrieved on behalf of the field.

s04.slug: MONDAY · 7:45 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE
body: On the lounge television, sound off, a man in a suit points a marker at a map of Florida, and under him the crawl says SAINTS · COLTS · TWO WEEKS TO MIAMI. On the screen a quarterback in a black-and-gold helmet throws a football at the sky in slow motion, over and over, and the sky declines to catch it. It has been on since dinner, for company.

It is a Monday-night lounge. Doug is cross-legged on the carpet with a mug of cereal; Kevin has the middle couch to himself and a BlackBerry he keeps turning over; Margot has the armchair, a legal pad on the arm and her Docs flat on the floor; Theo, in the blazer, takes the other couch lengthwise with one shoe on the cushion. Jack has the Greene open on his knee, the Penguin with the cracked spine, to a page where it is raining on a London common. He is still on the page he started on, which is a good page.

Priya goes past the open door with a roll of tape and a fresh laminate, THE ELEVATOR IS NOT A WAITING ROOM. THIS MEANS YOU, and stops in the frame to say, to the lounge at large, “It’s for the elevator,” in case anyone had taken it for the lounge. She goes on to the elevator.

Kevin has been waiting all evening to report, and when Doug asks what is wrong with his face, he reports: the oldest Dominguez brother, Javi, has invited him to a 49ers game. A home game. With the family.
“Dude,” Doug says. “It’s January. The season’s over.”
“September,” says Kevin. “I have time to prepare. I looked up the stadium. I looked up the *parking*.”

Jack was in the lot at St. Brendan’s at midnight on Saturday when the van came home, under the sodium light, and saw the handshake at the side door. “How long was the handshake, Kev?” Kevin looks at him. “It was a normal handshake.” “How long,” says Doug. Kevin consults the ceiling. “It was a long normal handshake,” he says, and goes red to the ears, and is furious about going red.

Margot has been writing since the Embarcadero. The piece is for the Newman beat, about the women on the route with the signs, and she has a first sentence she will not read to anyone. “It contains the word *nuns*,” she tells Doug, for the fourth time, “and no adjective. I had to work for that. I won’t be workshopping it with a lounge.
“The ones in the running shoes,” Jack offers.

“The shoes are in the second sentence. I will thank you not to compose my first.” She uncaps the pen. “On Wednesday the President addresses the nation. Does anyone propose to watch it, or are we all going to read about it in the *Times*, in the voice of a person who was in the room?”
“Is it a big deal, dude?” Doug asks. “Or is it like the Oscars?”
“It’s the Oscars, Pruitt,” says Theo, “where one party stands up and the other sits on its hands, and then they switch for the next paragraph.”
“I would like to see whether he mentions Thursday’s decision,” Margot says. “The Court sits ten feet from the podium, in its robes, obliged by decorum to look at its lap.”
“He’s allowed,” Jack says. “It’s a speech.”
“Is it? Or is it an ambush with applause lines?”

“To answer your question,” Jack says, “Hale’s. He moved Greene up from Thursday. Wednesday at six, his house, the speech on his television. Bring a guest. The wine’s cheap, and phones go in the dog’s bowl.”
“The dog’s bowl,” says Doug, reverent.
“Costigan’s plus-one,” Theo announces, “has been selected.”
“I haven’t asked anyone.”

“That’s what makes it a selection.” He swings his shoe to the floor. “I shall bring a bottle. A ninety-four Rioja Reserva out of my grandfather’s cellar in Pasadena, given to him in ’96 by a Spanish ambassador who wept at the bouquet and was reassigned within the quarter. It has a story. It’s in the original crate.”
“You’re nineteen,” Kevin says.
“I am not drinking it, Tran. I am transporting it. The professor says the wine is cheap; I take that as an invitation.”
“And the girlfriend?” Margot says, to the legal pad.
“I hadn’t —”
“Out of the question,” says Theo. “Skye Callender at that table is a second feature. Hale would stop the seminar to ask her for notes.”
“He’d cite her,” Kevin says.
“He’d *hire* her.”
“Dude,” says Doug, “can *I* come?”
“No, Pruitt.”
“Before that,” Jack says, because it will come out anyway, “I’ve got a lunch tomorrow. Studio City. Her mother and her publicist.”
“The Callender interview,” Theo says at once, and the lacquer is gone from his voice; it comes out short. “Don’t eat the bread.”
“What?”

“Debbie Callender once took a bread basket away from a grown man at a wrap party. I was twelve. I watched it from under a table.” He sits up. “She’ll ask after me. I’m Teddy to her; it’s the one thing she and my father agree on. Tell her I’m well, thriving, and in a fraternity.”
“Why would I tell her you’re in a fraternity?”
“Because she’ll be thrilled,” Theo says, “and it will buy you four minutes.”
In the corridor Laney goes past the lounge door at a walk, the pink BlackBerry held up before her, lit, and keeps going toward the stairs. Jack turns the page.
“She didn’t even look in, dude,” Doug says.
“Observe the omission, Douglas,” says Margot. “It takes more effort than looking.”

Theo has watched Laney go without turning his head. When he speaks again it is idly, with his eyes on the muted quarterback. “Picture it, Costigan. Hypothetically. February the seventh. The Saints, in the Super Bowl. A man who no longer attends Sully’s.” The shoe goes back up on the cushion. “Where does that man watch it?”

response: “A radio,” Theo says. “In 2010.” His thumbs go to the iPhone. “Noted. For the hypothetical.”
“Which side?” says Margot.
“Ours.”
Theo types something and won’t say what.
Theo nods, too slowly, and types. Kevin watches him type. Kevin says nothing, which costs him.

s06.slug: TUESDAY · 7:20 AM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE NEWS FEED
body: Light comes in under the blind in a bar and lies across Theo’s comforter and the Sigma Rho pin on the dresser. Hollis sits on the nightstand in his teacup, shell to the window, intact, and in the bed under the bar Theo lies on his back with the iPhone held straight up over his face, reading the News Feed aloud in the voice, every name given its full weight. It is twenty past seven. He has been awake since six. He has, it is clear, been saving it.
Jack is at the desk with a mug of instant coffee, which he holds in both hands and hasn’t drunk.

“For Kayla Ruiz,” Theo reads, “who is *so tired*. Lord, hear our prayer.” He scrolls. “For the Marisol Surf Club, who report conditions as *glassy*. Lord, hear our prayer. For a freshman on three who has lost a retainer and is offering a reward.” He scrolls once more, and the thumb stops, and the voice drops half a tone, for a name he means. “For Skye Callender, who has added a photograph.”

body: He doesn’t give the response. He swings the phone around instead and holds it out across the gap between the beds, at the full length of his arm and then, to be fair, farther.

It was taken from above, blind, at arm’s length: her eyes open and straight up into the lens, his shut, laughing, her bare legs, the flannel slid off her shoulder, her mouth at his jaw. There is nothing in it that couldn’t be on Facebook, and anyone looking at it would know what it is.

Jack knew there was a picture. At noon she looked at it, and laughed once, and laid the phone face down on her floorboards, and he didn’t ask. He did not know it was going anywhere. No one has ever shown him himself from above. The boy in it looks happy, and a little stupid with it, and Jack doesn’t mind either one. Under the picture the caption says *my friend from school*. It takes him a moment to place the phrase. A laugh goes through him, short, a cough in the wrong place, and Theo’s eyebrows go up.

“That’s me,” Theo says, tapping the line of names. “Theo Vance, first. I liked it at six. I’m being supportive.” He pulls the phone back and reads down the rest. “Kenzie Rourke, who liked it before she had finished the caption. Tyler Brandt, who likes everything; it’s a ministry. Doug Pruitt, who has liked it three times and been told by the website no.” He turns to the comment under it.

body: “Eleven people have liked that,” Theo says. “It is the most successful thing she has done in public, and she will be insufferable about it, quietly, until Easter. And at 12:02 Laney sent me the screenshot. With a caption.”
“What caption?”
“It’s a Texas word. I won’t use it in front of Hollis.” He scrolls on, up the page, with a flat, final thumb. “That’s everyone who spoke.”
Jack drinks the coffee now. It is stone cold, and he drinks all of it.
Theo lowers the phone to his chest. When he talks again the loglines are gone, and it comes out short. “That wasn’t aimed at you, Costigan.”
“No,” Jack says. “Corinne told her yesterday at six to take everything down.”
“The publicist.” Theo turns the word over. “There you have it. I’ve known her since eleven, and she has never heard a no she didn’t forward.”
Jack, who heard her say one yesterday at a quarter past twelve with both his wrists in her hand, doesn’t correct him.
“Theo.” He turns the empty mug around in his hands. “I think she’s the answer.”

Theo takes it lying down, which is how he takes most things before nine. Then he sits up against the headboard to receive it properly, with the iPhone face down on his chest. “The answer,” he says. “Costigan. It is twenty-five past seven on a Tuesday. You are holding cold Folgers in a Delgado mug. Nobody finds *the answer* over instant; it’s in the bylaws.” He considers. “Is there a pamphlet? I’ll want the pamphlet. I’ll want it framed.”
Jack doesn’t laugh, and Theo looks at him a beat past the end of the bit.

“People have asked her to be a lot of things,” Theo says, and it comes out short, with nothing on it. “I’ve watched them do it since we were both in braces. Nobody ever asked her to be that.” He looks at the ceiling, where the bar of light is. “It’s heavy, an answer. For the person you hand it to.”
And the voice goes back on, up into the nose and over the Alleghenies. “And now. Youngstown. For Tommy Hritz, of St. Christine’s.”

body: “That’s her third this month,” he says. “She’s working toward a vocation. Call her, Costigan.”
“Tonight,” Jack says. “She’s at school.”

In January he promised himself his mother would never again hear it from the Pallantes, and he kept it: he called her about the girl himself, first, from a gas station in Buellton, before he said yes to anything. Nobody told him there would be a photograph.
Theo regards him with real tenderness. “Your mother glued my name to a stocking,” he says. “I owe her a favor. I could call the school and tell her it’s a screenshot from a Sigma Rho prank.”
“Don’t.”
“I’m only describing my range.”

Under those the page goes on, and Theo goes down it at speed: a Dominic who wants to know if she’s tall; two aunts; a man who sold Frank a snowblower in 1998 and wishes it known that he always saw something in the boy; a girl from his Confirmation class, now at Kent State, who writes only *WOW*. They ask if she’s nice, if she’s Catholic, if he’s home for Easter. They ask about the jacket. Jack watches the wall go by like a street he used to live on, seen from a bus.

“And one friend request.” Theo turns the phone over to check. “An Ursuline sophomore you have never met. Her profile picture is a horse in a sweater. She has one mutual friend.” He holds the screen out. “It’s your sister.”
At 7:31 the RAZR on the desk goes off, and doesn’t stop. Gina writes in lowercase as a matter of principle. These are in capitals.

body: Ashley Vrabel is the weather in Gina’s life, and today there is weather. He has a quiet, appalled thought that is not about himself at all. She is fifteen, and she had to look at this in a chemistry room, with Ashley Vrabel holding the phone.
He shuts the phone. Theo says nothing; he gets up, takes the empty mug out of Jack’s hand, fills it from the illegal kettle on the windowsill, and gives it back.

At ten past eight Jack is in the hall in shower sandals with the caddy under one arm, and Kevin comes out of 420 with a mug of tea and the clipboard, takes one look at his face and winces, fully, before he can stop it.
“I’m not saying anything,” Kevin says. “Respectfully.”
“You’re wincing.”

“Wincing is anatomy, not commentary.” He considers the tea. “It’s a good picture. I’m not going to pretend it isn’t. That’s what makes it so hard to have an opinion about. Doug asked me if you can untag yourself.”
“Can I?”
“You can take your name off it. The picture stays. It’s a hospital wristband: you can cut it off, and the patient still got the procedure.”
“I’m not untagging.”
“I didn’t say you should. I said you can.”

He goes a few steps along the wall with the mug and comes back. “Also, I lied about you on Saturday. To Peter. I was terrible. He asked if you were sick and I said ‘spiritually,’ and then I had to keep going.”

The RAZR is still open in Jack’s hand to IM NOT TELLING MA. Rita Pallante put her question on his wall at six, his time, and for a woman who runs a church kitchen two hours is a long time to hold a casserole. Somewhere in Ohio a fifteen-year-old is at a desk with her own phone under it, presumably waiting.

s11.slug: WEDNESDAY · 11:25 AM · ANACAPA COMMONS — THE TABLET
body: It is early for lunch at the Commons, and the room is half full of people who have decided to be late for something. The television over the cereal bar is on CNBC with the sound off, a man in a tie explaining something to a ticker, and every few seconds the same four letters come around the bottom of the screen, AAPL, AAPL, the set stuck on a single name.
At the long table by the glass Theo has had the MacBook open to a live blog since ten, and he calls it aloud now, leaning into the turns. “And it’s *thin*. It’s thin, it’s thin, it’s —”
“How thin?” says Doug.
“Half an inch.”
“Of *what*?”
“A pound and a half. Nine point seven inches across. He has sat down in a chair to use it.” Theo’s hand goes to his chest. “The blog is moved.”
“The blog says the room laughed,” he goes on. “The blog does not say at what. The blog is as much in the dark as we are.”
“That,” says Margot, “is the most honest live blog ever filed.”
“And there’s a keyboard you dock it in. It *docks*, Pruitt. And it reads books.”
“Dude. Does it make calls?”
“It does not make calls.”
Doug takes this in as news of a death. “Then what is it *for*?”
“That is the beauty of it,” Theo says, with relish. “We have to be told.”
“Dude, can you carry it in a backpack?”
“It’s a pound and a half, Pruitt. You could carry it in a handbag.”
“I don’t have a handbag.”
“You will.”
“It is a large iPhone,” says Margot, “that cannot make a phone call.”

“It reads books,” Kevin says. “It’s a Kindle that went to college.” He has found a napkin and begun long division on it. “Four ninety-nine for the cheapest one. That’s a semester of orgo books. The two books and the lab manual.” He studies the napkin, and the books lose, and he looks stricken to have caught himself at it.

At the far end of the table Priya has the orgo text open flat beside her tray to a page of hexagons; the highlighter is capped, and the page stays where it is. “Viewing of tonight’s address in the Fishbowl is sign-up only,” she tells the table, in case it is about to be a different kind of table. “Pruitt, you are on the list. In pen.”
“Dude,” says Doug. “I love a list.”

Skye is beside Jack with her coffee and her sunglasses pushed up into her hair, and her knee against his under the table, and she has been there since the Commons opened, saying almost nothing and delighted by all of them, with the unguarded pleasure she takes in people who want nothing from her. She watches Doug’s face. When Doug, appealing at last to the one person present with a professional opinion, says, “Skye. You’re from Hollywood. What *is* it?” she doesn’t even look at the MacBook.
“It’s a placemat that knows things,” she says.
“*Dude*,” says Doug, with love.

The table has stopped treating her as a visit. Doug has given her his hash brown; Kevin has asked her, about Javi, whether Montana or Young; and Margot watches her with the sidelong suspicion she reserves for a sentence that is better than it has any right to be.
“The only open question,” Margot says, “is who will buy one and be ashamed.”
“I’d buy it if it came with a note from my mother saying I couldn’t,” Skye says.
Margot lowers the legal pad. It is as close as Margot comes to a standing ovation.
“You will hate it,” Margot tells Jack. “On principle.”
“I’ll hate it when there’s a Greene on it.”
“There is an iBooks,” says Theo.
“Then I’ll hate it in the same room as the Greene.” Skye steals the crust of his grilled cheese and eats it, looking at no one.
“Six o’clock, Costigan,” Theo says, over the lid. “I’ve pressed the blazer.”

Doug needs to know the size, so Jack takes a Commons tray off the stack and stands it on its end and frames a rectangle in the middle of it with his two hands — “About that” — and Doug leans in as if the rectangle might make a sound. The RAZR is lying open next to the syrup. Skye has the white iPhone out at arm’s length, back camera, blind, before he has finished the sentence.

body: “Liked,” says Theo, eyes on the MacBook.
“You can like a picture,” Doug marvels, “from the same *table*?”
“It’s called solidarity, Pruitt.”

Laney is at the next table over, behind Jack’s left shoulder, with a fruit cup and the pink BlackBerry face up beside it. Jack has the back of his chair to her. Skye, on his right, looks across his shoulder at the next table and gives it a small clear wave.
“Hi, Laney.”
“Morning,” Laney says, to the fruit cup.
Theo shuts the lid of the MacBook halfway, and says, at the volume of a back row: “You can’t know what a thing is *for*, Delaney, until somebody *tells* you.”
“Some people launch things without telling anybody, Theodore,” says Laney, “and everybody has to find out from the *internet*.”
Jack turns his head. They freeze: Theo with the lid at forty-five degrees, Laney with a cube of cantaloupe stopped on the fork in the air. Then they go on, worse.
“Which is why one waits for the facts, Delaney, before forming a view of the device.”
“I’ve been waiting for the facts since September, Theodore. Nobody sends them.”
“Perhaps the device is simply shy.”
“It had a whole keynote. It’s not shy, it’s scared.”
“Of what?”
“Of being a phone.”
“Dude,” says Doug. “It *isn’t* a phone.”
Skye has leaned in to Jack’s ear with her coffee up in front of her mouth. “They’re running lines,” she says, low.
“What?”
“Those two. That’s blocked. Who’s the audience?”
“Me, apparently.”
She looks at him over the rim of the cup. “No,” she says. “You’re the B camera.” And drinks her coffee.

He pushes the little pitcher of milk across to her elbow before she has looked for it, and she takes it without comment. Doug asks Kevin whether the iPad has a camera, and Kevin says that it doesn’t, and Doug says that’s crazy, who’s it for, and the question goes around the table again.

Laney stands with her tray in one hand and comes by behind Jack’s chair on the way to the dish return. Her free hand comes down on his shoulder, finds the collar of the flannel turned up on the left, and flattens it with one smooth pass of her palm. She is two steps on before she stops. Her back goes rigid. She walks again, faster, and sets the tray on the belt hard enough to rattle the forks.
Jack puts a hand up to the collar. “Did Laney just —”
“It was the wind,” says Theo.
“We’re indoors,” says Margot.
“It’s a draft.”
“From the dish return,” says Doug, “dude?”
“It’s a very powerful dish return, Pruitt.”
Skye watches Laney all the way to the dish window, with interest.
Theo closes the MacBook the rest of the way and folds his hands on the lid. “Verdict, Costigan,” he says. “The tablet.”

“He has a flip phone,” Skye says. “He’s very pure.”
“Can it make calls though,” says Doug.
